title: Former UNH police chief hired as Greenland police captain after DUI conviction - WMUR

Former University of New Hampshire police Chief Steven Lee has a new job in law enforcement months after pleading guilty to a DUI charge. The Greenland Police Department announced on Facebook that Lee was sworn in as police captain Thursday. Lee resigned from UNH earlier this year following his January arrest in Portsmouth on a misdemeanor charge of driving under the influence. He later pleaded guilty, paid a fine and completed a state-approved impaired driver education program. As a result, his driver's license suspension was reduced from nine months to three months. Lee's hiring comes about six months after his arrest. The former NHL player's change of plea hearing was continued to July 24. Photo taken July 10, 2026 BARNSTABLE, Mass. — A hearing for former NHL player Eric Nickulas to change his plea in Barnstable Superior Court has been continued to July 24. Judge Michael Callan approved the delay Friday. Nickulas, of West Barnstable, was arrested on Sept. 11 at a Hyannis apartment complex after police say he tried to rendezvous with someone he thought was a 16-year-old girl but was actually a Barnstable police detective. He was charged with enticement of a child under 18 by using electronic communication. Detectives were on hand when Nickulas arrived at the Hyannis apartment complex where the meet-up was supposed to be held. He was taken into custody without incident, according to police reports. A grand jury in Barnstable Superior Court returned two indictments against him on Sept. 24, charging him with electronic enticement of a child for commercial sexual activity and pay for sexual conduct with a child under 18. On July 6, Nikulas' attorney Peter Lloyd filed a request for a charge concession and sentencing memorandum. According to Boston Lawyer Blog, a charge concession occurs when the state agrees to reduce the charge against a defendant in exchange for a guilty plea or other concessions. A “sentencing memorandum” is a document submitted to the judge before sentencing to advocate for a sentence. One charge carries a maximum prison sentence of not more than five years or a fine of not less than $2,500, or both. The second charge carries a maximum prison sentence of not more than 10 years in prison, a fine of not less than $3,000 and not more than $10,000, or both, whether such sexual conduct occurs or not. Born in Hyannis, Nickulas played hockey for Barnstable High School and a variety of private schools before attending the University of New Hampshire where he played for four years. He signed with the Boston Bruins in 1998 and played until 2001, then from 2005 to 2006. He played for the St. Louis Blues and Chicago Blackhawks from 2002 to 2004. title: UNH Stock Becomes Dow’s Biggest Driver Back To 50,000 — Will Trump Tailwinds Spark Another Leg Higher? - Stocktwits
content: Shares of UnitedHealth Group (UNH) have emerged as the biggest driver of the Dow Jones Industrial Average’s return toward 50,000, turning a battered healthcare giant into one of Wall Street’s hottest comeback trades. UNH stock has surged 47% since Feb.10, making it the best-performing Dow component over the same period and outpacing even AI winners, including Amazon’s 31% gain, Caterpillar’s 22% rise, Nvidia’s 20% jump, and Cisco Systems’ 18% gain. UnitedHealth entered the year under pressure after soaring medical costs, Medicare Advantage reimbursement changes, and a collapse in profit guidance rattled investors last year. Now, the healthcare firm says a turnaround is coming earlier than expected. At Bank of America’s Healthcare Conference this week, CFO Wayne DeVeydt said that first-quarter results pointed to “a very strong year” if conditions hold. He said Optum Health, a major drag last year, is now “performing better than expected, sooner than expected.” Optum Health posted $1.3 billion in adjusted operating profit with margins of 5.4%, ahead of analyst expectations. Bank of America Securities (BofA) later raised its price target on UNH shares to $420 from $380, implying a 5% upside from current levels. The bank cited “bullish” discussions at the conference, saying UnitedHealth is increasingly confident it can return most businesses to at least the low end of their target margin ranges by 2028. The company is still working through fallout from Medicare Advantage changes that UnitedHealth previously said could create a $6 billion hit this year. UnitedHealth has responded by renegotiating contracts, trimming its workforce, reworking benefits and divesting clinics. The company said membership losses are now tracking in line with projections and not as severe as worst-case scenarios. UnitedHealth’s rally has also picked up a political tailwind. U.S. President Donald Trump’s latest filings showed multiple UNH purchases during the first quarter, including a trade valued between $100,001 and $250,000 on Jan.23. Additional filings showed smaller UNH purchases on Jan.12, Feb.23, March 17 and March 23, along with a separate purchase valued between $50,001 and $100,000 on March 18. DeVeydt said UnitedHealth expects to invest $1.5 billion into AI this year and is already generating at least a two-to-one return on those investments, with payback periods under 12 months. “Our confidence level is growing by the day around the benefits we are seeing,” he said. The company said AI is central to redesigning healthcare administration, automating claims processing and simplifying prior authorization systems. UnitedHealth has already rolled out AI-based tech across clinics, automated coding systems and real-time adjudication tools. The company also said it plans to reduce prior authorization requirements by 30% and process all authorizations in real time by the end of 2027. The AI strategy centers around Optum Health and Optum Insight, which UnitedHealth sees as long-term growth engines capable of driving both margin expansion and new software revenue streams. Optum Rx recently unveiled a “transparent, fee-based” pricing model to move away from traditional rebates. The move also comes as the pharmacy-benefit-manager industry faces mounting regulatory scrutiny over rebates and drug pricing. Meanwhile, the company plans to repurchase at least $2 billion of stock by the end of the second quarter under existing authorization. Boost Run, which operated six U.S. data center locations, with five additional locations in progress, had a market capitalization of $450 million as of Thursday, making it significantly smaller than rivals. On Monday, the company disclosed that it had about $940 million in contracted customer revenue and expects to achieve $375 million in annualized revenue by the end of this year. Intuitive Machines (LUNR) is on track to extend its winning streak into a third consecutive week on Friday, after touching a three-year high in the previous session as the company moves toward becoming a diversified aerospace infrastructure operator with expanding commercial and government exposure. Shares of AST SpaceMobile (ASTS) and Rocket Lab (RKLB) are in the spotlight early Friday after fresh filings from U.S. President Donald Trump showed purchases in both space firms, alongside several major chip and communications stocks. ASTS stock jumped 11% on Thursday, and RKLB shares advanced 8%. The new filings released on Thursday showed that Trump bought between $1,001 and $15,000 worth of ASTS shares on March 17, while disclosures showed a larger $15,001 to $50,000 purchase in RKLB stock on Jan.21. The filings also revealed positions in Alphabet, Intel, Qualcomm, Texas Instruments and Corning. Investors viewed the basket as a broader bet on satellite broadband, launch infrastructure, AI defense systems, communications networks and semiconductor demand, particularly as Trump continues pushing his proposed Golden Dome missile-defense initiative. The system is expected to require large-scale satellite deployment, orbital tracking infrastructure, interceptor systems, secure communications networks and defense electronics, fueling investor interest across space and defense equities. The renewed attention comes after AST SpaceMobile’s latest earnings report intensified concerns around satellite deployment timelines. The company reported a quarterly loss wider than Wall Street estimates, while revenue also missed expectations. Although the company maintained its full-year revenue outlook, investors focused heavily on manufacturing and launch execution risks. Satellite communications consultant Tim Farrar said after the earnings call that AST SpaceMobile’s assumptions may not support its target of placing 45 satellites in orbit by year-end. He argued that the company would likely require multiple rapid launches from both Blue Origin and SpaceX to hit the goal. Concerns intensified after BlueBird-7 failed to reach its intended orbit during Blue Origin’s New Glenn Mission-3 launch following an upper-stage anomaly. AST SpaceMobile later said the satellite is expected to de-orbit and that insurance should cover the loss. However, investor sentiment improved after AST SpaceMobile disclosed that three BlueBird satellites are scheduled for a mid-June Falcon 9 launch. The company also said 32 satellites are already in advanced stages of assembly and reiterated its plans to launch every one to two months on average. The company also highlighted government and defense opportunities, including potential exposure to Golden Dome-related programs and Space Development Agency contracts. President Scott Wisniewski said AST SpaceMobile sees a potential revenue opportunity nearing $1 billion in 2027, driven largely by contracted and recurring revenue streams. RKLB, meanwhile, has become one of Wall Street’s biggest Golden Dome trades. On Thursday, Rocket Lab revealed that the U.S. Space Force Chief of Space Operations General Chance Saltzman recently visited the company. The fresh focus also followed a Congressional Budget Office estimate projecting that Trump’s Golden Dome initiative could ultimately cost as much as $1.2 trillion over the next two decades, with a major portion expected to go toward space-based interceptor systems and satellite networks. During its latest earnings call, CEO Peter Beck said Rocket Lab was already supporting missile-warning systems, missile-tracking programs, hypersonic testing and Space-Based Interceptor initiatives connected to Golden Dome. Rocket Lab also disclosed that the company, alongside RTX Corporation, was selected for interceptor development work, while its Haste hypersonic launch platform secured a $190 million Department of Defense contract. Investor optimism got a further boost after Rocket Lab said that its 1,000th Rutherford engine had rolled off the production line, reinforcing confidence in Electron launch scalability. On the other hand, demand for Neutron remains strong. Neutron is the company’s larger reusable rocket targeting constellation deployment and national-security missions. While ASTS stock has jumped 216% over the past year, RKLB stock has rocketed 449% over the same period. For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com. Ondas (ONDS) has drawn intense attention as the stock eyes its best week in four months, fueled by a blowout fiscal first-quarter (Q1) earnings report that seeks to reframe the AI-powered autonomous drone systems developer’s growth prospects. During the Q1 earnings call, Ondas Chairman and CEO Eric Brock said the company’s strategy now spans air, ground, and stratospheric technologies tied to defense, security, and infrastructure markets. “Our plan is working. Over the past year, we laid out a clear core plus strategic growth strategy to build Ondas into a scaled global operating platform for unmanned and autonomous systems serving defense, security, industrial, and critical infrastructure markets,” said Brock. Brock said Ondas is growing by acquiring companies, developing new products, and expanding into global markets. He explained the company’s strategy as a “systems of systems” approach, in which it develops technology in-house and acquires other businesses to strengthen its defense and industrial capabilities. Wednesday was Ondas’ best day in 2026, with the stock rallying over 26%. At the time of writing, the stock pared gains and traded over 1% lower overnight. Brock explained that revenue growth in Q1 was fueled by strong demand for counter-unmanned aircraft systems and defense-related technologies, including contributions from Sentrycs Cyber-over-RF platforms and Iron Drone interceptor systems. The company experienced explosive growth in Q1, with revenue of $50.1 million, marking a more than tenfold increase from last year. The company also reached a key operational milestone as its product divisions achieved adjusted EBITDA profitability during Q1, approximately six months ahead of internal targets. Ondas also increased its full-year 2026 revenue forecast to at least $390 million, reflecting a 670% year-on-year increase. As of the end of Q1, the company held approximately $1.48 billion in cash and cash equivalents, providing flexibility to fund growth, pursue additional acquisitions, and advance its Core + Strategic Growth Program. title: UNH Vs. HUM: Which Insurer Stock Has More Upside After CMS Reverses Wall Street’s Biggest Medicare Rate Fear? - Stocktwits
content: Shares of UnitedHealth, Inc. (UNH) and Humana, Inc. (HUM) are back in the spotlight on Tuesday after the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) lifted Medicare Advantage payment rates for 2027, with Wall Street estimates pointing to a clear frontrunner. UNH stock rose 8% in extended trading, while HUM stock gained 11%. Over the past year, however, UNH has fallen about 45% and HUM nearly 27%, with both stocks underperforming the broader Health Care Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLV), which climbed 10% over the same period. The CMS finalized a 2.48% increase in Medicare Advantage payment rates for 2027, up from the January proposal that kept rates roughly flat and wiped out nearly $100 billion in market value across major insurers. The updated policy is expected to add more than $13 billion in additional funding to Medicare Advantage plans next year, the CMS said. With the policy overhang removed, attention has shifted back to valuation targets, which point to higher implied upside for UnitedHealth than for Humana. Based on Koyfin estimates, UnitedHealth carries a 12-month average price target of $357.81, implying a 27% upside from the stock’s last close. Coverage across 29 analysts includes 7 ‘Strong Buy’, 16 ‘Buy’, 4 ‘Hold’ and 2 ‘Sell’ ratings. Earlier this month, Raymond James upgraded the stock to ‘Outperform’ with a $330 price target, citing potential upside from expense trends and expected margin improvement at Optum Health, the company’s care delivery arm. Meanwhile, Bernstein SocGen Group reiterated an ‘Outperform’ rating with a $405 target, pointing to UnitedHealth’s expanding AI strategy. The company recently launched its generative AI companion, Avery, as part of broader efforts to reduce operating costs across its insurance segment, where it plans nearly $1 billion in expense cuts and is closing or divesting about 550 Optum Health clinics. UnitedHealth also expects to lose as many as 2.8 million insurance members this year, with revenue potentially declining for the first time since the 1980s as longtime chair and former CEO Stephen Hemsley leads a turnaround effort. The stock still remains below the level at which Warren Buffett’s Berkshire Hathaway built its stake last year and faces scrutiny over Medicare Advantage risk-adjustment practices following a Senate committee review. Humana’s upside appears more modest based on Koyfin estimates, with a 12-month average price target of $212.17, implying a 16% upside from current levels. Among 27 covering analysts, the stock carries 2 ‘Strong Buy’, 6 ‘Buy’, 17 ‘Hold’ and 2 ‘Sell’ ratings. Earlier this year, the company projected adjusted 2026 earnings of at least $9 per share, below consensus expectations of $11.87, while the insurer said margins in its individual Medicare Advantage business could remain just below break-even this year. Several brokerages subsequently lowered price targets, with UBS and BofA maintaining ‘Neutral’ ratings after Humana’s 2026 EPS outlook came in roughly 24% below consensus. On the other hand, Morgan Stanley warned that uncertainty around the size of Humana’s 2026 membership cohort remains a risk “particularly heading into 2027 and beyond.” Cantor Fitzgerald said the stock may remain range-bound until clearer membership data emerges in the second quarter, and Guggenheim said it was taking “a prudent view” of the company’s 2027 earnings outlook. Still, Humana expects enrollment in its individual Medicare Advantage plans to increase about 25% in 2026 compared with last year, with over 70% of new members coming from competing plans. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment for UNH and HUM was ‘extremely bullish’ amid ‘extremely high’ message volume. One user said UNH “was $600 a year ago. One of the safest blue chips to double In a couple years.” Another user noted that “this $13B increase provides critical revenue relief, offsetting rising medical costs and securing sector stability.” For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com. Meanwhile, Marvell shares jumped after expanding a partnership with Nvidia through the NVLink Fusion ecosystem, boosting the company’s position in next-generation AI infrastructure. Nvidia also disclosed a $2 billion investment in Marvell. Separately, Erste Group initiated coverage of Marvell with a ‘Buy’ rating, citing continued profit growth, improving return on equity and strong positioning in optical DSP and custom silicon used in AI systems. TSLA stock fell more than 2% on Monday, marking its lowest level in nearly seven months. GLJ Research analyst Gordon Johnson said on X that Tesla has broken below its 20, 50 and 75-day moving averages and remains trapped in a descending channel that began after the stock’s December highs near $480. He added that Fibonacci levels point to $322 as the next key support, while momentum indicators indicate the stock is not yet oversold. He also lowered 2026 earnings per share (EPS) estimate to $1.8 from $2, below consensus expectations, citing risks to demand, execution and competition as Tesla expands into lower-priced, higher-volume vehicle segments. The company produced 408,386 vehicles during the quarter. Model 3 and Model Y deliveries totaled 341,893 units, while Model S, Model X and Cybertruck deliveries reached 16,130 units. Tesla also deployed 8.8 gigawatt-hours of energy-storage products, down from 10.4 gigawatt-hours a year earlier and below estimates. The results come as the U.S. electric-vehicle market adjusts to the phase-out of federal purchase incentives and competition from Chinese automakers intensifies across markets. content: The Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF (SCHD), a cornerstone for many dividend-focused investors, just completed its annual index reconstitution, with changes becoming effective on March 23, 2026. This isn't just a minor tweak; it's a significant rebalancing act that saw 25 new companies added to the portfolio and 22 existing holdings removed, fundamentally altering the ETF's sector composition and underlying characteristics. This annual process ensures SCHD continues to track the Dow Jones U.S. Dividend 100 Index, which rigorously screens for high-quality dividend stocks. The most pronounced shift is a substantial reduction in energy sector exposure, which dropped by roughly 8%. This move is a deliberate effort to trim commodity-driven volatility, as energy had reached an unusually high weighting of around 20-21% in the fund. Conversely, the reconstitution bolstered allocations to sectors like Healthcare (up 4%), Technology (up 3%), and Financials, which is expected to reclaim its position as a dominant sector within the ETF. Among the notable additions are industry giants such as UnitedHealth Group (UNH), Qualcomm (QCOM), Abbott Laboratories (ABT), Procter & Gamble (PG), and Accenture (ACN). These companies are known for their strong market positions, consistent cash flows, and reliable dividend growth. On the flip side, the fund bid farewell to names like Valero Energy (VLO), Halliburton (HAL), Cisco Systems (CSCO), and AbbVie (ABBV), among others, as they no longer met the index's stringent quality and dividend sustainability criteria. This rebalance isn't merely about swapping out old names for new ones; it's a strategic recalibration designed to reinforce SCHD's core mandate: delivering sustainable, growing dividends from high-quality companies. The index’s rules-based approach, which emphasizes metrics like cash flow to debt ratios, return on equity, and consistent dividend histories, ensures that the portfolio remains aligned with its long-term objectives. For investors, this means a potentially more diversified and less volatile income stream going forward. The significant sector rotation within SCHD's portfolio is a direct consequence of the index's rules-based methodology, which prioritizes quality, dividend sustainability, and financial health. Energy, despite its strong performance in recent periods, saw its allocation reduced from an elevated 20-21% to potentially as low as 12-15%. This isn't a punitive measure against the sector, but rather a reversion to historical norms, as energy's weighting has typically hovered in the 5-10% range, peaking around 15% shortly after SCHD's 2011 launch. Lower energy prices throughout 2025 likely impacted the financial metrics of some energy companies, triggering their removal. Conversely, the Financials sector is poised for a comeback, with its weighting expected to rise from 9.7% to 15% or more. This shift reflects improving metrics and attractive yields among financial institutions, many of which now qualify under SCHD's criteria. Financials often thrive in normalized interest rate environments and offer defensive qualities through diversified revenue streams, making them a natural fit for an income-focused ETF. Their inclusion enhances SCHD’s exposure to a sector historically undervalued relative to its earnings power, without sacrificing the ETF’s core income focus. Technology also received a modest bump, increasing its exposure by 3%. While not traditionally a high-dividend sector, the ongoing AI revolution has seen a growing number of tech companies mature into dividend payers with robust cash flows. The addition of names like Qualcomm (QCOM) reflects this trend, bringing in companies with strong balance sheets and solid dividend profiles, even if their earnings growth has been volatile in the short term. This strategic increase in tech and healthcare exposure (up 4%) helps balance the portfolio, reducing reliance on any single sector and potentially enhancing overall stability. This sector reshuffle strengthens SCHD's foundation by reducing commodity-driven volatility and boosting diversification. The index's emphasis on quality ensures new entrants bring comparable or superior dividend-growth trajectories, often sustaining or even lifting the portfolio’s overall payout trajectory. It’s a proactive adjustment that positions SCHD for improved performance and resilience in a normalizing economic environment, demonstrating the adaptive nature of its passive management strategy. The inclusion of UnitedHealth Group (UNH) and Qualcomm (QCOM) into SCHD's refreshed portfolio represents a strategic move to infuse the ETF with robust dividend growth, sector diversification, and strong underlying fundamentals. These aren't just any dividend payers; they are market leaders in their respective industries, bringing a blend of stability and growth potential that aligns perfectly with SCHD's mandate. QCOM's presence diversifies SCHD's tech exposure beyond traditional names like Texas Instruments. Both UNH and QCOM are S&P 500 constituents, signifying their large-cap status and market importance. No immediate action is required on your part, as SCHD automatically adjusts its portfolio to reflect the new index composition. The shift away from a heavy energy weighting towards increased exposure in Healthcare, Technology, and Financials is designed to enhance diversification and reduce commodity-driven volatility. While energy had been an elite performer in 2026 leading up to the reconstitution, this move prevents any single sector from dominating and keeps the portfolio aligned with its long-term quality criteria, which has historically delivered an annualized total return of roughly 13% with lower volatility than the broader market. title: Ruth White named top America East outdoor track scholar-athlete of the year - Bangor Daily News
content: Maine news, sports, politics, election results, and obituaries Orono native and standout distance runner Ruth White became the eighth University of New Hampshire woman to be named America East Women’s Outdoor Track and Field Scholar-Athlete of the Year. The 20-year-old White earned All-America honorable mention honors by finishing 22nd in the 10,000-meter run at the NCAA Division I Outdoor Track and Field Championships at the University of Oregon last month. She posted a time of 33:11.62. The sophomore finished second in the 10,000-meter run at the America East championships with a time of 33:55.29 and was ninth in the NCAA Division I East event with a season-best time of 33:08.83. The top 12 finishers from the Division I East race advanced to the nationals. White, who has a 3.98 cumulative grade-point average in mechanical engineering, set the school record in the 5,000-meter run in April with a time of 16:03.28 at the Friar Invitational in Providence. She also won the 5,000-meter run at both home meets. She concluded the outdoor season with the fastest America East woman’s time in the 10,000-meter run and the third-fastest in the 5,000. The 4-foot-8 White did not run during the indoor track season. White participated in four cross country events last summer and fall, winning three and finishing third in the 25-team New England Intercollegiate Amateur Athletic Association meet at Hopkinton, New Hampshire, in October but she never ran another cross country meet including the America East championships. She also didn’t run during the indoor track season after finishing third in the 5,000 meters and fifth in the 3,000 meters at the 2025 America East Indoor track championships. White had an exceptional freshman season, winning the America East outdoor title in the 10,000 meters with a time of 32:57.83; finishing sixth in the NCAA Division I East race (32:50.17) and then earning second team All-American status with her ninth-place showing at the NCAA Division I championships (32:20.60). White was a three-time Gatorade Cross Country Runner of the Year at Orono High School and was an All-American. title: UNH crews search Lake Massabesic for missing WWII B-17 ball turret - UnionLeader.com
content:
Mostly clear. Low 59F. Winds light and variable.. A University of New Hampshire autonomous mapping boat searches for remnants of a World War II-ear B-17 Flying Fortress in Lake Massabesic. Research project manager Andy McLeod prepares to launch the University of New Hampshire’s autonomous mapping boat to search for remnants of a World War II-era B-17 Flying Fortress at the bottom of Lake Massabesic in late June. Research project manager Andy McLeod walks to the University of New Hampshire’s autonomous mapping boat before he launched it to search for remnants of a World War II-ear B-17 Flying Fortress in Lake Massabesic. University of New Hampshire student Kate Murray gestures toward monitors in a research trailer while searching for remnants of a World War II-era B-17 Flying Fortress in Lake Massabesic. Alex Saidel, a local aviation history enthusiast, watches from a research trailer as a group from the University of New Hampshire deploys an autonomous mapping boat to search for remnants of a World War II-ear B-17 Flying Fortress in Lake Massabesic. University of New Hampshire student Ashley Riz Advincula watches the monitors in a research trailer as and autonomous mapping boat searches for remnants of a World War II-ear B-17 Flying Fortress in Lake Massabesic. Historian Dennis Sasseville speaks with a reporter about the search for remnants of a World War II-ear B-17 Flying Fortress in Lake Massabesic. University of New Hampshire student Ashley Riz Advincula watches monitor in a research trailer as an autonomous mapping boat searches for remnants of a World War II-ear B-17 Flying Fortress in Lake Massabesic. Research project manager Andy McLeod holds up the one of the remotes for the University of New Hampshire’s autonomous mapping boat as it sets sail to search for remnants of a World War II-ear B-17 Flying Fortress in Lake Massabesic late last month. Research project manager Andy McLeod, left, and University of New Hampshire student Tion Uriam prepare to launch an autonomous mapping boat to search for remnants of a World War II-ear B-17 Flying Fortress at Lake Massabesic. A rare copy of the Declaration of Independence found a new home after South Jers… The Londonderry Town Council took some steps to address traffic and safety conce… Research project manager Andy McLeod with the Center for Coastal and Ocean Mapping / Joint Hydrographic Center from the University of New Hampshire - Chase Ocean Engineering Lab and UNH student Tion Uriam (right) do a final check before launching a yellow battery powered uncrewed (robotic) surface vessel (USV), as it heads out to search Lake Massabesic for a ball gun turret dumped off a WWII B-17 Flying Fortress and into the water below following an aborted landing attempt at Grenier Air Base (known today as Manchester-Boston Regional Airport) in January 1945. Living near Lake Massabesic, Alex Saidel grew up hearing stories of the history lying somewhere below the surface. “I always heard there was either a World War II plane or parts here or something like that, but that was always the end of it,” said Saidel, an aviation buff and president of Merrimack Street Volvo. “But what if we can find it?” Over the past few weeks, teams from the Center for Coastal & Ocean Mapping/Joint Hydrographic Center, based at the University of New Hampshire’s Chase Ocean Engineering Lab were at Lake Massabesic, working with Saidel while searching for a ball gun turret from a B-17 Flying Fortress. The turret was jettisoned from the bomber following an aborted landing attempt during a training flight out of Grenier Air Base — known today as Manchester-Boston Regional Airport — in January 1945. Crews hope to find and raise the turret to the surface using cables and flotation devices, tow it to shore and restore it for display in the Aviation Museum of N.H. “Today, almost no physical trace remains of Grenier Air Base, which once housed thousands of troops from all over the nation as they trained for missions in Europe and all over the world,” said Jeff Rapsis, the museum’s executive director. “Displaying the ball turret would provide Aviation Museum visitors a tangible connection to Grenier Air Base and Manchester’s role during World War II.” The story of this search begins not 60 feet below the surface of Manchester’s drinking water source, but in a car dealership. When Dennis Sasseville — a local historian and aviation history enthusiast — showed up at Saidel’s Volvo dealership, as luck would have it, the salesmen were busy with other customers, and Saidel assisted him with finding a car for him and his wife. Sasseville himself was familiar with the story of a B-17 ball turret in Lake Massabesic after reading a mention of it in author Ed Brouder’s book, “Manchester’s Airport: Flying Through Time.” “I said, in the era of internet let’s do some more research. So, I found that there was an accident report,” Sasseville said. “At that time you could send away to a database for $25 or $30 and get the actual photocopies of the Army accident report. I did that and did a little bit more research, and over the years I would tell fellow amateur historians about it, and most of them kind of shrugged their shoulders and said, ‘Well, that’s nice.’” When it came time to put pen to paper on his car purchase, Sasseville noticed a lot of World War II memorabilia in Saidel’s office. “We get talking about World War II and he’s actually flown a restored B-17,” Sasseville said. “I said, ‘Well you know there’s this ball turret in Massabesic Lake’ and his eyes just lit up.” He reached out to the University of New Hampshire, and the hunt was on. Since about mid-June, engineers and experts from UNH have been focused on locating the ball turret from the B‑17 aircraft (serial number 44-6694). The plane, which belonged to the 99th Bombardment Group, was reportedly en route to Tortorella Air Base in Foggia, Italy, when the gun turret was intentionally dropped into the lake after a failed landing attempt at Grenier Field. The tailwheel broke off, making a second landing attempt dangerous. The B-17 ball turret is affixed to the underside of the fuselage in a way that could break the back of the fuselage when touching down without landing gear (dubbed a belly landing). According to the accident report, the pilot was told to “Drop the turret into the lake.” Working with staff from Manchester Water Works, UNH crews set up a mobile control van along the shore of the lake. From there, they operated a battery-powered, robotic uncrewed surface vessel (USV) outfitted with a M3 Multibeam Echosounder — on loan from KONGSBERG, one of the university’s industry partners — to assist with the exploration efforts. A small Garmin side-scan sonar provided acoustic “imagery” of the lakebed. The advanced high-resolution multibeam sonar allowed the team to collect data for 3D topographic maps, while the Garmin side-scan provided acoustic shadows of objects that could be the turret. Inside the trailer, graduate students in UNH’s summer hydrographic field course took part in the search, giving them a unique opportunity to explore a local body of water for a historical artifact. The class is composed of graduate students from the United States and around the world enrolled at the center, recognized as the nation’s premier Category A Hydrographic mapping training program. Val Schmidt, principal research project manager and UNH team lead, said work like this on an inland lake is new for him. “My office has been this picnic table for the last two weeks. It’s been terrific,” Schmidt said. “We do a lot of stuff off the coast as part of the class and for different things. So it’s not uncommon offshore, but I don’t know of another project that we’ve done in a lake.” Professor Semme Dijkstra, a UNH research scientist at the School of Marine Sciences and Ocean Engineering, said the school is training graduate students from across the U.S. and the world to survey the ocean floor. This year’s class has 10 students. Schmidt said each weekday morning students and staff have been coming out to the trailer near the Water Works Treatment Plant off Lake Shore Road, setting up, having a morning meeting and mapping the lake bed while looking for anything that might be the turret. “They come with a plan about what they want to do for the day and we help them execute it,” Schmidt said. That plan typically involves deploying the boat around 9:30 a.m., launching what Schmidt calls a lawnmower survey because it travels back and forth along equally spaced lines across the lake. A University of New Hampshire autonomous mapping boat searches for remnants of a World War II-ear B-17 Flying Fortress in Lake Massabesic. “They’ve laid out a strategy of where they think the turret is most likely to be, so they’re prioritizing those spots and trying to get full coverage,” Schmidt said. “They program the boat by drawing these lines out on a map and then they can push a button and the boat will just go and run them. Then they monitor the data collection effort as it’s coming in and try to pick out targets or things that we want to go investigate later.” At the end of a wooden dock, research project manager Andy McLeod and UNH student Tion Uriam did a final check on the yellow USV before the day’s run began. “This is a fairly new machine for us, and generally speaking we can do about six to eight hours of ops,” McLeod said. Have their efforts raised any eyebrows among neighbors or folks out on the water? “Maybe the loons, but I haven’t seen anybody come over and get all upset about us,” he said. Back in the trailer, Roland Arsenault — the vehicle’s chief software engineer, monitored a mosaic of camera images tiled across two large monitors. “That’s our side-scan sonar on the left,” Arsenault said. “This is water column, like your fish-finder-type sonar on the right. Here is the map that we use to navigate the boat to plan our missions and to see where we are. And these are the cameras — the boat has four cameras, forward, sides and rear.” Lake Massabesic has a storage capacity of approximately 15 billion gallons of water and covers 2,400 acres, or about four square miles. The lake averages only about 17 feet in depth across its entirety, with the deepest area checking in at approximately 60 feet near Front Park by the Massabesic Yacht Club. Schmidt said the team worked with Alex and Dennis to come up with areas of the lake to focus on. “Just thinking about what you would do if you were a pilot — you probably didn’t want to get near the trees, you don’t want to hit houses or the shoreline. The accident report from the Air Force — there’s very little detail in there about where they were exactly, and where they dropped it and what their strategy was when they dropped it,” Schmidt said. Research project manager Andy McLeod holds up the one of the remotes for the University of New Hampshire’s autonomous mapping boat as it sets sail to search for remnants of a World War II-ear B-17 Flying Fortress in Lake Massabesic late last month. According to the Army Air Force’s accident report, at the time of the accident, “the runways were covered with patches of ice and braking action was fair.” “Due to this condition the pilot of this aircraft made his approach so as to land as short as possible,” the report says. “In doing so his main gear made contact with a snow bank. Seeing what had happened the pilot pulled back on the stick in order to go around again and this caused the tail to be forced down, hitting the snow bank with sufficient force to shear off the tail wheel.” In his statement on the accident, 2nd Lt. Douglas E. Sherman (the pilot) wrote that the tower instructed him and other crew members to “fly over to a lake 4 or 5 miles to jettison the ball turret.” “We went over to the lake and circled while the crew loosened it up,” Sherman wrote. “As soon as the tower instructed us to let it go, we were flying at 1,000 (feet) around two lakes, so we wouldn’t go over any houses. When it left, we were over the lake and I went in. We called the tower and told them the turret was gone and we proceeded back to the field for a wheel landing.” Alex Saidel’s research shows B-17 #44-6694 was originally delivered to Nashville, Tennessee, on Oct. 15, 1944. From there she went to Hunter Army Air Base in Savannah, Georgia, arriving Dec. 8, 1944, before flying to Grenier Field on Jan. 4, 1945, where she was assigned to the 416th Bomb Squadron of the 99th Bombing Group. After dropping the ball turret, the B‑17 aircraft was repaired and sent to Tortorella Air Base in Foggia, Italy, on Feb. 11, 1945, before ultimately taking part in 36 missions between Feb. 22, 1945, and April 26, 1945. The aircraft survived the war and was retired to Bradley Field in Connecticut on July 15, 1945. She was then sent to Independence Airfield in Kansas on July 17, 1945, before being sent to a scrap yard at Kingman, Arizona, on Dec. 21, 1945. The tale of the turret isn’t the only well-worn New Hampshire-based yarn involving a World War II aircraft. Hikers can view the scattered wreckage of a Douglas B-18 Bolo Bomber at Mount Waternomee in Woodstock. The aircraft crashed into the mountain on Jan. 14, 1942, during a blizzard. Five of the seven crew members survived after being rescued by residents of Woodstock and Lincoln. As of this writing, the missing ball turret hasn’t turned up, though Rapsis said the search itself is just as important as finding the relic. “History has so much to teach us, and not just in books,” Rapsis said. “It can be found all around us — sometimes under water. Even if the effort to retrieve the ball turret is ultimately unsuccessful, the search for it is a reminder that all those who answered the call to serve their country in World War II should not be forgotten.” Share your opinion with New Hampshire. title: Former UNH police chief who pleaded guilty to DWI hired as Greenland police captain - UnionLeader.com
content:
Mainly clear. Low 59F. Winds light and variable.. A Nashua woman has been sentenced to seven days in jail afte… FALL RIVER, Massachusetts — A Bristol County Superior Court … Former University of New Hampshire Police Chief Steven Lee, who pleaded guilty to driving under the influence following his arrest earlier this year in Portsmouth, has been hired as a police captain in Greenland. The appointment was approved unanimously by Greenland’s Selectboard following “a comprehensive review of his career, qualifications, and recent personal journey,” town officials said in a statement Friday. Greenland officials said they recognize that members of the public “are familiar with Captain Lee because of his highly publicized DWI arrest earlier this year.” “Rather than avoid that reality, we believe it is important to address it openly,” the statement said. “Captain Lee accepted responsibility for his actions and has completed all consequences associated with that violation. The Town of Greenland did not make this hiring decision in spite of these events, rather we made it after carefully considering them. “We believe accountability is demonstrated by acknowledging mistakes and that true character is often demonstrated by how a person responds to adversity.” Selectboard Chair Laura Malloy said the unanimous vote “reflects our confidence in Steve Lee’s exceptional career.” “Leadership is not measured by whether someone has ever failed,” Malloy said. “It is measured by how they respond when they do. Steve accepted responsibility, held himself accountable, sought meaningful help, and emerged from the experience a stronger person and leader. Those are qualities we value, and we are proud to welcome him to the Town of Greenland.” Lee, 50, of Dover, was driving a black 2017 Ford Explorer owned by UNH when he was stopped on the on-ramp of Interstate 95 south at Market Street at 12:29 a.m. on Jan. 22, according to a police narrative obtained by the Union Leader through a Right-to-Know request. Under the terms of his plea, Lee was ordered to pay a $620 fine, had his driver’s license suspended for nine months and was directed to take part in a 20-hour Impaired Driver Education Program, court records show. According to the police report, an officer stopped Lee after observing his UNH-owned SUV “repeatedly going over the white dotted lines into the right lane.” “At one point there was an 18-wheeler in the right lane, the SUV did swerve over the dotted line coming close to colliding with the 18-wheeler,” the police report says. “The SUV then over corrected and swerved back into their lane then going over the yellow solid line.” Lee partially failed field sobriety tests and declined to take a breathalyzer test. Lee resigned his position as UNH police chief effective April 1, after being notified through his counsel on March 25 that UNH was terminating his employment following an investigation into his arrest. title: Ex-UNH chief named Greenland police captain after DUI arrest - AOL.com
content: GREENLAND — Former University of New Hampshire police chief Steven Lee, arrested in January for driving under the influence in Portsmouth, has been hired as a police captain in Greenland. The town's Board of Selectmen voted to approve Lee's appointment in a late June non-public session. Lee, sworn in Thursday, July 9, is now the Greenland Police Department's first-ever captain, ranking second-in-command to Chief Wayne Bertogli, according to Town Administrator Tara Tucker. "Our whole justice system is supposed to be about reducing recidivism and learning our lesson … With the amount of experience and knowledge he has, it's an amazing pickup for Greenland," Tucker said in a Friday, July 10, interview. Portsmouth police charged Lee on Jan. 22 with a single Class B misdemeanor count of driving under the influence on Market Street. Lee was placed on paid administrative leave from UNH, with Capt. Mark Collopy was named the school's interim chief. More: UNH police chief on leave after DUI arrest in Portsmouth After initially contesting the charge, Lee pleaded guilty in early February, roughly three weeks after his arrest, to avoid trial. Lee was operating a UNH-owned Ford Explorer with firearms in the vehicle at the time of his arrest in Portsmouth, per reporting from the Concord Monitor. Under his original plea conditions, according to court records, the 50-year-old career law enforcement official's license was suspended for nine months, though after Lee's participation in an impaired driver care management program, his license suspension was reduced to a three-month term. Lee was also ordered to pay a $620 fine. The amended terms of Lee's license suspension were approved by Portsmouth District Court Judge John Pendleton in late April, a few weeks after Lee's formal resignation from UNH. Lee's tenure in law enforcement spans over 30 years, many of which were spent at UNH. A former state liquor enforcement officer, Lee was involved in a July 2007 police chase that ended with the death of a 22-year-old motorist in Kittery, Maine, though he was cleared of any wrongdoing. That same year, Lee took a full-time officer role in the UNH police force, shortly after he was involved in an investigation into after-hours drinking at a Dover bar. A 2007 Foster's Daily Democrat report notes Lee did not break any laws. In Greenland, Lee, an FBI National Academy graduate, was hired as police captain, a new role that was restructured from a vacant lieutenant position in the department, which has nine full-time personnel. The job remained open after Bertogli, then a lieutenant, was promoted to chief last fall to replace Tucker, the town's police chief since April 2012 following the fatal shooting death of Michael Maloney in a Post Road drug raid. Bertogli and town selectmen reviewed Lee's career accolades, his recent self-reflection and participation in the state-approved impaired driver care management program. "The achievements that he has made over the years are just incredible," Bertogli said in an interview Friday. "The dedication to law enforcement that he has had over the years, we looked at that and said one bad mistake doesn't ruin a person, provided they take accountability and try to move forward." "Our unanimous vote reflects our confidence in Steve Lee's exceptional career," Board of Selectmen chairperson Laura Malloy said in a prepared statement Friday. "Leadership is not measured by whether someone has ever failed. It is measured by how they respond when they do. Steve accepted responsibility, held himself accountable, sought meaningful help, and emerged from the experience a stronger person and leader. Those are qualities we value, and we are proud to welcome him to the Town of Greenland." At UNH, Lee replaced Paul Dean, the school's longtime former chief who took a position in New Hampshire Gov. Kelly Ayotte's administration after retiring from the university. Lee was not immediately available for comment Friday. That same year, Lee took a full-time officer role in the UNH police force, shortly after he was involved in an investigation into after-hours drinking at a Dover bar. A 2007 Foster’s Daily Democrat report notes Lee did not break any laws. In Greenland, Lee, an FBI National Academy graduate, was hired as police captain, a new role that was restructured from a vacant lieutenant position in the department, which has nine full-time personnel. The job remained open after Bertogli, then a lieutenant, was promoted to chief last fall to replace Tucker, the town’s police chief since April 2012 following the fatal shooting death of Michael Maloney in a Post Road drug raid. Bertogli and town selectmen reviewed Lee’s career accolades, his recent self-reflection and participation in the state-approved impaired driver care management program. “The achievements that he has made over the years are just incredible,” Bertogli said in an interview Friday. “The dedication to law enforcement that he has had over the years, we looked at that and said one bad mistake doesn’t ruin a person, provided they take accountability and try to move forward.” "Our unanimous vote reflects our confidence in Steve Lee's exceptional career," Board of Selectmen chairperson Laura Malloy said in a prepared statement Friday. "Leadership is not measured by whether someone has ever failed. It is measured by how they respond when they do. Steve accepted responsibility, held himself accountable, sought meaningful help, and emerged from the experience a stronger person and leader. Those are qualities we value, and we are proud to welcome him to the Town of Greenland." At UNH, Lee replaced Paul Dean, the school’s longtime former chief who took a position in New Hampshire Gov. Kelly Ayotte’s administration after retiring from the university. Lee was not immediately available for comment Friday.
